"title": "Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries",

"executive_summary": "The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries is a vital but poorly-understood class of materials, combining organic and inorganic components, and it allows a battery to function by protecting electrode materials from unwanted side reactions. The authors note that key questions about SEIs, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them, remain unanswered, limiting the development of next-generation batteries. Existing methods are inadequate: pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers, and even the fastest useful DFT methods are much too slow to study the time and length scales of the SEI. Hybrid functionals such as wB97X that yield improved barrier heights struggle with metals and have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. The authors therefore use a combination of classical sampling and a novel machine learning model to produce the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy, to be used in future machine learning applications and compared to experimental results. They describe a model and sampling procedure that describes the interaction of these materials and thus permits the ranking of candidate SEI structures. The model is a multitask-trained QRNN (a machine learning force field) trained on multiple levels of theory, including GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and a SPICE organic-chemistry subset. They used multiple rounds of active learning for data generation, enhanced reaction sampling using Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) on the QRNN potential energy surface, and a supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the latent space via multitask training. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrodinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics and reaction templates applied at intervals. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, giving a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. They defined four sets of candidates with different levels of added Li: 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box. Having produced a series of unique initial geometries, they annealed them using their reactive QRNN model with NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each, and ranked each set of candidates by calculating the mean potential energy of each structure over an MD trajectory of 20 ps length at ambient conditions of 300 K and 1 atm. The difficulty of characterizing the SEI system experimentally is a strong motivation for this work, but also an obstacle to validation, because experiments do not exist for any SEI composition. Instead, they validated their model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers. They generated the first plausible ranking of SEI candidate structures, along with analysis of hypotheses related to SEI composition. They refer to the lowest-energy SEI candidate structure out of the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms) as predicted by wB97X-D3BJ output head as their \"best\" candidate. They performed statistical analysis of the bonding in SEI candidate structures by recalculating the Lewis structure of the entire system based on the atomic positions after reactive MD, then tabulating the counts of various bond types versus the total system energy. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. They have demonstrated that multitask training with a QRNN model, combined with sampling of relevant chemical systems, allows a machine learning force field to model the complex reactions characteristic of an SEI. They constructed SEI candidates using only a single formulation of electrolyte, 1M LiPF6 in EC, and suggest that the full power of this technique will come from comparing multiple formulations. Future work should include the application of other model architectures, including Nequip and MACE as well as architectures which allow the use of atomic partial charges such as CHGNet. They note that MLFFs offer a powerful opportunity to understand SEI materials, but only if we are willing to tolerate working in an environment where theoretical and experimental references are currently limited and the probability of being proven wrong by future events is high.",

summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.field_subfield: Materials informatics / machine learning force fields for battery interphases
summary.type_of_paper: Methodology + candidate-generation study (ChemRxiv preprint, not peer-reviewed)
summary.executive_summary: The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries is a vital but poorly-understood class of materials, combining organic and inorganic components, and it allows a battery to function by protecting electrode materials from unwanted side reactions. The authors note that key questions about SEIs, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them, remain unanswered, limiting the development of next-generation batteries. Existing methods are inadequate: pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers, and even the fastest useful DFT methods are much too slow to study the time and length scales of the SEI. Hybrid functionals such as wB97X that yield improved barrier heights struggle with metals and have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. The authors therefore use a combination of classical sampling and a novel machine learning model to produce the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy, to be used in future machine learning applications and compared to experimental results. They describe a model and sampling procedure that describes the interaction of these materials and thus permits the ranking of candidate SEI structures. The model is a multitask-trained QRNN (a machine learning force field) trained on multiple levels of theory, including GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and a SPICE organic-chemistry subset. They used multiple rounds of active learning for data generation, enhanced reaction sampling using Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) on the QRNN potential energy surface, and a supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the latent space via multitask training. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrodinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics and reaction templates applied at intervals. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, giving a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. They defined four sets of candidates with different levels of added Li: 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box. Having produced a series of unique initial geometries, they annealed them using their reactive QRNN model with NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each, and ranked each set of candidates by calculating the mean potential energy of each structure over an MD trajectory of 20 ps length at ambient conditions of 300 K and 1 atm. The difficulty of characterizing the SEI system experimentally is a strong motivation for this work, but also an obstacle to validation, because experiments do not exist for any SEI composition. Instead, they validated their model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers. They generated the first plausible ranking of SEI candidate structures, along with analysis of hypotheses related to SEI composition. They refer to the lowest-energy SEI candidate structure out of the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms) as predicted by wB97X-D3BJ output head as their "best" candidate. They performed statistical analysis of the bonding in SEI candidate structures by recalculating the Lewis structure of the entire system based on the atomic positions after reactive MD, then tabulating the counts of various bond types versus the total system energy. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. They have demonstrated that multitask training with a QRNN model, combined with sampling of relevant chemical systems, allows a machine learning force field to model the complex reactions characteristic of an SEI. They constructed SEI candidates using only a single formulation of electrolyte, 1M LiPF6 in EC, and suggest that the full power of this technique will come from comparing multiple formulations. Future work should include the application of other model architectures, including Nequip and MACE as well as architectures which allow the use of atomic partial charges such as CHGNet. They note that MLFFs offer a powerful opportunity to understand SEI materials, but only if we are willing to tolerate working in an environment where theoretical and experimental references are currently limited and the probability of being proven wrong by future events is high.

They note that MLFFs offer a powerful opportunity to understand SEI materials, but only if we are willing to tolerate working in an environment where theoretical and experimental references are currently limited and the probability of being proven wrong by future events is high.

Research Context
The SEI is a vital but poorly-understood class of materials combining organic and inorganic components. An SEI allows a battery to function by protecting electrode materials from unwanted side reactions. Key questions about SEIs, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them, remain unanswered, limiting the development of next-generation batteries. An SEI is a complex chemical structure that forms over large length and time scales, and involves conductors, insulators, and redox reactions; no existing method is fully applicable to the task of simulating such a system. Pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers. Even the fastest useful DFT methods are much too slow to study the time and length scales of the SEI. Hybrid functionals such as wB97X that yield improved barrier heights struggle with metals and have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. MLFFs promise to allow atomistic simulation with the accuracy and wide applicability of DFT, but with the fast sampling of classical force fields. Multitask learning lets us train MLFFs to both pure and hybrid DFT labels simultaneously. MLFFs can already predict properties of Li metal and of organic liquids.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central goal is to produce the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy for future ML applications and comparison to experiments. The authors hypothesize that a multitask-trained reactive MLFF can model the complex redox reactions characteristic of an SEI. They hypothesize that P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. They predict that adding a general organic chemistry dataset shapes latent space without heavy cost on model capacity. They predict that GFN1-xTB is the most suitable reference for generating charge labels for SEI training sets. They predict that the full power of the technique will come from comparing multiple electrolyte formulations. They predict that stable dynamics are achievable despite extreme conditions, which is often not the case for MLFFs. They predict that the dataset can be efficiently extended with a wider variety of reaction data.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on the SEI in lithium-ion batteries, using a single electrolyte formulation of 1M LiPF6 in EC. The reference level of theory for non-periodic systems is wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD. The reference level of theory for periodic systems is PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis. A random subset of non-periodic systems was labeled with PBE-D3 to improve information exchange between output heads. Periodic systems were not labeled with wB97X-D3BJ due to its great expense. Unlike previous QRNN models, theirs did not use GFN2-xTB atomic partial charge labels or DFT dipole labels. They tested reference atomic partial charges from GFN1-xTB, GFN2-xTB, and GFN0-xTB. They used multiple rounds of active learning for data generation to increase accuracy. They used enhanced reaction sampling using AFIR and NEB on the QRNN potential energy surface. They added a general organic chemistry dataset, SPICE, using elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P. Adding SPICE data caused only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. They doubled the width of the hidden layers to increase model capacity as they added more disparate data. They used a higher-priority dataset of periodic and cluster surface reaction subset, sampled half per batch (as in rehearsal). They applied decoupled weight norms with the norms not included in the optimizer. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrodinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, giving a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. Each system runs with a unique random seed for packing and for MD, ensuring the sampling of many configurations. They defined four sets of candidates with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box. They annealed initial geometries using reactive QRNN NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each. They ranked candidates by mean potential energy over a 20 ps MD trajectory at 300 K and 1 atm. Because each set of candidates has the same number of atoms of each element, the system energies are directly comparable.

Procedures And Architectures
The model is a multitask-trained QRNN (machine learning force field) trained on multiple levels of theory. The loss function consists of energy and atomic force mean squared error for each level of theory in each training batch, plus charge mean squared error. Charges are not separated into different output heads, with all levels of theory using consistent charge labels. They had four output levels of theory: GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and SPICE wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPPD. The first and last output heads were only used to shape the latent space during training, not for prediction on SEI systems. They used the Adamax optimizer with decoupled weight decay. They used a learning rate of 2e-3 for the final model. They used only 1% of the data as the validation set, selected uniformly at random. They used hidden layers of size 256, 224, and 192 for all elements. Their batch size was 64. A high weight decay of 3e-3 per batch was helpful but reduced reaction barrier heights, so they used 1e-3 for the final model. The final model was an exponential moving average of training parameters, averaging every 10 batches with alpha = 0.001. They used NPT ensemble for 1 ns to obtain equilibrated density for liquid systems. For solid-liquid interfaces, they started from a BCC lattice of lithium with an initial spacing of 2 Å. No constraints were applied to the lithium slab; the lithium was allowed to participate fully in the dynamics. They added lithium oxide, lithium carbonate, lithium fluoride, and lithium hydroxide to the training set. They sampled non-equilibrium geometries by adding Gaussian noise to the Cartesian coordinates of the original geometries. They used Quantum Espresso with PBE functional, D3 dispersion correction, and a plane wave energy cutoff of 40 Ry. They used a 3x3x3 k-point mesh for bulk supercells and a 3x3x1 k-point mesh for surface supercells. For NEB with periodic systems, they used lithium surfaces with 54 atoms topped with a single EC molecule. They extracted clusters within 3-6 Angstroms from reacting atoms for non-periodic labeling with wB97X-D3BJ. They chose a radius around each central atom from a uniform distribution from 3.0 to 5.2 Å, plus a 1.2 Å buffer for hydrogen atoms. They did not use DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries as training inputs.

Key Results
The authors produced the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. They validated their model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers. They could not compare density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus against experimental values because such experiments do not exist for any SEI composition. They refer to the lowest-energy SEI candidate structure out of the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms) as predicted by wB97X-D3BJ output head as their "best" candidate. They performed statistical analysis of bonding by recalculating the Lewis structure of the entire system based on atomic positions after reactive MD. They tabulated the counts of various bond types versus the total system energy. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable structures. The QRNN models gave stable dynamics despite the extreme conditions applied, which is often not the case for MLFFs. Adding SPICE data did not increase PBE-head validation RMSE on the battery datasets. The most stable SEI candidate for each formulation could allow calculation of Li+ diffusivity and mechanical properties. The authors note that this is the most complex redox reactive system simulated using an MLFF or any method of comparable accuracy.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The latent space of these MLFF models contains unused capacity that can be applied to broadening chemical applicability. They recommend the use of a supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the latent space via multitask training as part of future MLFF works. The result implies that the greatly increased scope of the data did not impose a heavy cost on model capacity. The finding that GFN1-xTB achieves the best compromise between accuracy and convergence across isolated and periodic systems supports its use for charge labels. The association of P-F and Li-O bonds with stability suggests these bonds stabilize the SEI. The association of C-O and Li-F bonds with instability suggests these bonds destabilize the SEI. The ability to model complex redox reactions implies MLFFs can handle systems previously out of reach. The finding that the full power of the technique will come from comparing multiple formulations implies future work should generalize across electrolytes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that the difficulty of characterizing the SEI system experimentally is also an obstacle to validation. They could not compare density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus against experimental values because such experiments do not exist for any SEI composition. They note that they do not regard their current model as final, since its scope is still small compared to what is required. They constructed SEI candidates using only a single formulation of electrolyte, 1M LiPF6 in EC. They note that a higher weight decay reduced the height of their reaction barriers relative to the reference barriers. They note that the probability of being proven wrong by future events is high. They note that they focused on a relatively small part of reactive chemical space, the known decomposition reactions of EC. They note that they did not sample these reactions on other surfaces, such as lithium oxide or lithium carbonate. They note that the random seed for packing and MD is not reported in detail. They note that the exact settings for the SPICE level of theory are not fully detailed.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
They tested reference atomic partial charges from GFN1-xTB, GFN2-xTB, and GFN0-xTB. They found the older GFN1-xTB to be the most suitable for generating charge labels for SEI training sets. They found little effect of early stopping validation for this dataset. They found that a high level of weight decay was helpful in producing smoother energy surfaces with faster convergence. They note that another useful technical extension would be to test models trained with only subsets of the dataset used here.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy, generated via multitask-trained reactive MLFF sampling. 2. The strongest evidence is that adding a general organic chemistry dataset shapes the latent space without heavy cost on model capacity, with only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. 3. The future path is to compare multiple electrolyte formulations and apply other model architectures such as Nequip, MACE, and CHGNet.
